For those who don't know, this is the Trolley Problem. I know cars are not trolleys; this is just an example. Cars will face their own problems.

Cars will be self driving. The computer will be able to process insane amounts of information in a split second. If confronted with an either or situation, it will have to be programmed with rules on how to respond. Programmers will make these decisions. Let's say a child and an adult step into the road from opposite sides at the same time. Which one will the car decide to hit? Man or woman? Old to young? One brilliant scientist or two less brilliant scientists? Two kids vs one kid and one adult? Obviously the list goes on.

When an accident occurs, and it can be proven that the computer chose one person over another, I imagine the dead person's family will want to discuss this in court. How will these decisions get made? Are we ready for that? Will ethicists be hired by car companies? Will the government make the rules?
How will self-driving cars handle ethical decisions akin to the trolley problem?

While I am by no means a developer for self-driving cars, I am more than positive that for self-driving cars to become street-legal, they have built-in mechanisms and algorithms that predict the movement of objects in their surroundings to completely avoid getting stuck in such situations. However, given that this is real life and that algorithms fail when presented with an input they were not meant to handle, my way of handling ethical decisions like those would be to minimize the overall damage. From a driver's perspective, it's impossible to know that some lives are more valuable than others, so by calculating which direction will minimize the number of people that can get hit and slamming on those brakes, it's possible to solve the ethics problem. However, you have to assume that this is a 100% black and white situation, and in real-life, the drivers will most likely be able to take manual control of the car if everything just goes completely haywire and there are options to just crash your car because you shouldn't be going fast enough to die in such an event if there are pedestrians to hit and if you were wearing your seat belt and so on.

I wouldn't be surprised if, initially, the cars won't even be able to tell between say, a small kid and a dog or some other animal. I think it would come down to mass and the possibility of harm to the occupants. That's honestly the car software's chief concern, right? Preservation of the passengers in the car. In that scenario it'll compare a big object to a small object and choose the small one.

But if we're really trying to make things better, the answer is obvious. Both of them; what are they doing in the street? Get outta the gene pool. /s

Unfortunately this is close too how it will probably have to be done. The simplest choice for the algorithm is to stop. Obstacle recognition as a neural network application is still resource intensive without specialized hardware. Conversely, If the time to recognize an obstacle takes a long time, they may have optimized the algorithm towards path prediction to give a longer breaking time.

Like you said, you have very little real time to determine what to do. So, you're going to code for the most conservative approach. Determining whether something is a paper bag or a boulder is not only computationally complex and intensive, it's also a dangerous thing to get wrong. What if you decide the boulder is a paper bag this time and keep driving? You hit the giant rock and have a horrific wreck. Accuracy rates that are totally okay for facebook's facial recognition aren't okay for a self-driving car.

So, no, I don't think cars are going to be making ethical decisions any time soon.

Despite this very real fear, roads would be safer, and there would be no more phantom traffic. The best way to solve this problem is to avoid it completely with early detection, and with enough automatic cars on the road, a network of information relaying back and forth between cars with the position of every person / sizable living being on or near the road at all times. While it would be very computationally complex to determine the difference between certain objects, there is no need to know excruciating details for everything that's detected. The computer would only need to know object's size, density, and whether or not they are living things. For every corner case that cannot be determined for whatever reason (weather, solar radiation, you name it) AND the early detection system failed, the car should be smart enough to ask for human input with enough time to help differentiate a boulder from a child from a paper bag, etc.

Oh, I'm not afraid of it. I have no problem with cars not making ethical decisions. We've already got countless controls in place to allow the safe coexistence of pedestrians, bicycles, and automated cars. Guess which of those are going to violate those controls? My point is - the car will conservatively do whatever it can to safely avoid an accident. It may not always be completely avoidable, but it won't be the fault of the car.

I wouldn't make a lot of assumptions about the ease with which the density or "aliveness" of an object could be determined. I'd also point out that there are going to be driving situations wherein the "network" of cars is useless. Remote mountain roads with blind corners where obstacles fall into the road and your car is the first to see it. I'd also strongly caution against the wisdom of having networked cars. I understand the dream, but the threat of exploitation is huge.

Adding to this, note that if the computer can not react in time, the driver sure can't either.

Also, a scenario I expect to see in the future includes the computer killing the driver as the better outcome (Running him off the road).

I expect to see media shitstorms with uneducated people raging, blaming the software for not being perfect. But honestly, while accidents will happen, I think travel by car will be a whole lot safer than it is now.

As for security requirements, my own expectations would be that the software can valuate between people and less important obstacles along with amount. - I.e. be able to avoid or minimize expected human casualties. As a software developer, I can certainly say this would be possible. Estimation of age could possibly be included, but beyond that, the car should not be choosing anyone over anyone else.

It's going to see you a hundred yards away and start to track you. If you start getting close to the road it is going to slow down and make a wide birth around you same way a human would. As in your example where a child and an adult step out onto the road at the same time, the car would have seen them from far away and would be going slow enough (because it was unsure of what their intent was) that it could easily stop before hitting the pedestrians. If the car cannot stop before hitting something, it's probably because that thing is coming at the car fast enough that the car cannot out maneuver it, it which case it's not really the car's fault. They can't dodge bullets.

If a self driving car is going to crash, it's no longer a matter of what it has been programmed to do. It would continue to do it's best not to crash until it crashes, what it hits will be depending on variables such as proximity.

There's simply no way that in the split seconds before a crash the car will be able to use facial recognition or whatever to bring up all every potential person involved in the upcoming crashes info to make an informed choice between people or anything like that. Realistically the cars will instead have a harm minimization algorithm that will see the potential for mass injury and/or death and will choose to take the path that spares the most people. If it's got to choose between the occupant, an adult and a child and there's simply no way to avoid that decision then the simple solution is to pick the easiest path to save two lives. One may die but two will live and if people don't find that appealing the easiest way to avoid conflict is for the car to enter an emergency mode where it must be manually driven. If it does that then it becomes a human decision who to hit and it would also likely remove any liability from the car manufacturer too. My guess is that they go down that path initially but end up with complete automation due to it being safer for everyone.
